money_at_stake.rationale: Re-appraised 2026-08-30 after adversarial verification found roughly 85% of a 36-appraisal batch citing sources that did not support their claims. Fetching every cited URL this run found three of the four original evidence items did not survive: the GlobeNewswire Pure DC (Finland) citation timed out on four WebFetch attempts and two curl attempts (TLS handshake succeeds, server never answers within 25s) and has no Wayback snapshot, so it is unverifiable rather than disproven. The CNBC Stargate Norway citation opened cleanly (HTTP 200) but does not support the claim as written: the article states Nscale and Aker EACH committed around $1 billion to the initial 20MW phase of the site, not $1 billion combined to a 230MW phase, and states no $250 million equity figure or 290MW expansion anywhere in the piece; deleted rather than repaired with the real, smaller figures, per this pass's rule against softening an unsupported claim to fit. The Seeking Alpha Nvidia-matchmaking citation returned HTTP 403 directly, and its one Wayback snapshot (20260822004222) is currently unreachable, Internet Archive self-reporting temporarily offline: unverifiable this run. What survives is the single Microsoft/Nscale/Aker deal: a signed five-year, $6.2 billion agreement securing Microsoft AI-compute capacity from a data center in Kvandal, in Norway's Narvik region, 230MW initially and expandable to 520MW, with the five-year contract set to begin in 2026 (RCR Wireless, fetched and quoted this run). That single cited figure sits inside the $1-10B band, not $10-100B, so the band moves from B10_100 to B1_10. This is not a finding that the other three deals are fictitious, only that this appraisal no longer asserts a number for them without a source it has actually opened.

public_reach.rationale: Re-scored on the evidence that survived this run's fetch pass; held at 35. The Statnett/2.3GW grid-queue claim in the prior version does not appear anywhere in its cited source: the Data Center Knowledge article it was attached to discusses Denmark's Energinet (roughly 60GW of new grid connection requests, about 14GW tied to data centers, against roughly 7GW of peak demand), never Norway's Statnett and never the figure 2.3GW. That evidence item is deleted, and the state-gatekeeper argument is dropped from this rationale since nothing on file supports it for Norway. What remains points the same direction as before: the parties actually named in the one surviving deal are 'U.K.-based Nscale' and 'investment company Aker' with Microsoft as customer (RCR Wireless), none of which is itself a listed pure-play; Nscale's own financing runs through a $790 million bank-led package, a $2 billion Series C and a $1.4 billion delayed-draw term loan (Data Center Knowledge), all private-capital instruments rather than public equity; and the cleanest listed exposure stays one layer removed, Nvidia's roughly 90% share of an estimated $180 billion 2026 GPU/accelerator spend line (Introl), a global capture that does not move with this Nordic siting decision specifically. Held at 35: removing one unsupported state-actor claim does not change that the deal's own named parties are private and the direct listed sliver (an Aker ASA equity stake, Equinix colocation build-out) remains unsized.

capture_odds.rationale: Re-scored on the evidence that survived this run's fetch pass; held at 45. For capture: Nvidia's roughly 90% share of AI accelerator spend, about $162bn of an estimated $180bn 2026 GPU/accelerator line (Introl), is genuine concentration and qualification lock-in, the textbook shape of pricing power. Against capture: Nordic banks are underwriting Nscale's Norway campus as long-duration industrial infrastructure tied to energy access rather than pricing it like a scarce tech asset (Data Center Knowledge), a regulated-return signal rather than a moat signal. The prior version's additional argument for staying off the commodity floor, a claimed 2.3GW Statnett grid queue, is deleted: the cited source discusses Denmark's Energinet, not Norway's Statnett, and states no such figure anywhere. Without it, the score rests on the two-sided evidence above alone, which still lands near the middle rather than the floor: Nvidia's own product stays scarce and qualification-locked even where the site-level financing looks commodity-like, so 45 stands, on narrower grounds than before.

timing_fit.rationale: Re-scored on the evidence that survived this run's fetch pass; held at 80. The Pure DC Finland item is deleted as unreachable (see money_at_stake), so this leg now rests only on the Microsoft/Nscale/Aker deal: a signed five-year, $6.2 billion contract for AI compute capacity, set to begin in 2026 (RCR Wireless). That is already contracted rather than proposed and lands inside the 2 to 5 year horizon this repo underwrites, supporting the same score as before. Not scored higher because the deal's own stated expansion to 520MW carries no delivery date and may fall in the back half of the window or beyond it.

notes.text: This occurrence is an ambient CAND- candidate, not a promoted signal, so it carries no occurrence{} block: candidates.json rows have only a plain `date` field. anchor_date above is that field (2026-08-19), and there is no occurrence.window to check agreement against; check_impact.py's CAND- path only requires occurrence_id to resolve in candidates.json, which it does. LEAKY here is not a recommendation to drop this candidate: the candidate's own note that it sits inside the already-chained ai-infrastructure chain's power-cost-arbitrage link means a chain build was never going to start from zero here. What this appraisal adds is that the specific Nordic-siting money (Nscale's JV structure, bank infrastructure debt) is mostly private even though the region's deal flow is real and well evidenced; Nvidia's own capture is real but tracks its global GPU dominance rather than this Nordic-specific siting decision, so it is not incremental reach created by this occurrence.
